Adadelta.description:
Adagrad's idea, bounded by a window instead of a sum.

`rho` is the length of that window and is the parameter that keeps the step from
shrinking to nothing. Formulated to need no learning rate at all, though torch still
takes one and this specification still carries it - so a run that leaves
`learning_rate` at its default is not using the original method.

BoundaryLoss.description:
A region loss plus a term that knows how far a wrong voxel is from the truth.

Dice and IoU count a voxel the same wherever it sits, which is why a model can reach
0.88 on Dice while its volumes run a fifth too large: the overshoot is all at the
boundary, and for a small lesion the boundary is most of the object. This adds
`mean(phi * p)`, where `phi` is the signed distance to the truth's boundary.

```yaml
loss:
  name: boundary
  region: {name: focal, gamma: 2.0}
  alpha: 0.5
```

`alpha` weights the region term, `1 - alpha` the surface term. It cannot be 1, which
would leave the surface term doing nothing and the name lying, and it cannot be 0: the
surface term alone has no notion of how much of the object was found and is minimised
by a confident prediction deep inside a shrunken one.

**What it buys and what it costs, measured.** Against Dice alone on lesions with
ambiguous edges, three seeds, at the default `alpha`: the systematic volume bias goes
from -5.18% to -0.06%, and the per-case absolute volume error goes the wrong way, from
16.90% to 22.17%. Dice itself falls by 0.011. So it trades *accuracy per case* for
*being unbiased over a series* - and which of those you want is the question being
asked. "Is there a lesion" wants the overlap; "has it grown since March" wants a volume
that is not systematically wrong, and no single number answers both.

The bias improvement is suggestive rather than established on three seeds, because the
baseline's own bias wanders by ±3.11%. The costs are established.

**It also costs time.** The signed distance transform runs per sample in the loader's
workers - measured at 5.3 ms for a 256x256 image, 23.4 ms for a 64x64x32 volume and
709.8 ms at 128^3 - so on large volumes give the loader workers, or the transform
becomes the training.

alpha.description:
How much of the objective is the region term, `1 - alpha` the surface term.

**0.9 because 0.5 was measured and is unusable.** Three seeds on lesions with ambiguous edges, 60 epochs:

```
                 Dice             volume bias       volume |error|
dice alone       0.9525 ±0.0027   -5.18% ±3.11%     16.90% ±0.90%
boundary a=0.5   0.9164 ±0.0240  +32.22% ±28.28%    42.95% ±19.12%
boundary a=0.9   0.9411 ±0.0093   -0.06% ±4.15%     22.17% ±2.88%
```

At 0.5 the surface term has half the objective while the prediction is still random, which is where it is known to be unstable - the seed spread is six times the baseline's and every number is worse. Kervadec schedules this downwards from near 1 rather than fixing it; 0.9 is the closest a single number comes, and the spec deliberately has no schedule to hide behind.

Excludes both ends: at 1 the surface term is absent and the name is a lie, and at 0 nothing measures how much of the object was found.
alpha.title: Alpha

CceDiceLoss.description:
The blend to start a segmentation run with.

Cross-entropy keeps the gradients healthy while everything is wrong, Dice pulls the
overlap up once the easy voxels are done. `cce_weight` is the split, and at 0 or 1 it
is one of the two alone - which is worth knowing before tuning it as if it were a
third thing.

cce_weight.description: How much of the objective is cross-entropy; the rest is Dice. Cross-entropy cares about every pixel and Dice about the overlap, so raising this helps a class that covers very little of the image and lowering it favours the shape.
cce_weight.title: Cce Weight

CceLoss.description:
Per-pixel classification, with no notion of the object.

Healthy gradients from the first epoch, which the overlap losses do not have while
everything is still wrong. The cost is that it optimises what is numerous: with a
background of 95% of the voxels, which in medical images is ordinary, it is mostly
learning the background. That is what `cce_dice` exists to fix.

label_smoothing.description: Train towards 1 - this value instead of towards 1, so the model is not pushed to be certain. Worth having where the labels themselves are uncertain, which on a hand-drawn boundary they are.

ClDiceMetric.description:
Whether the structure is connected, rather than whether the voxels coincide.

The one metric here that measures a property of the whole mask: it scores the overlap
of the prediction's skeleton with the truth's, so a vessel broken into two pieces loses
where Dice barely notices. Measured on a constructed pair - a vessel drawn two voxels
thinner, against the same vessel cut in half - Dice reads 0.8750 and 0.9474 and so
*prefers* the severed one, while this reads 1.0000 and 0.9425 and does not. Both pairs
are pinned by a test.

**What it was worth on a real model**, FIVES, 200 cases: correlation 0.9779 with Dice,
mean difference +0.0041, 127 cases higher and 73 lower. At that quality it is not
telling a different story - which is itself the result, and the reason to read both.

Not a drop-in. A one-voxel structure displaced by one voxel scores 0, the skeleton
needs a whole mask so a tiled run reports it per case through `evaluate_cases`, and it
is absent from the per-epoch history for the same reason.

include_background.description: False here where the other metrics default to True, and not for the usual reason. The background's skeleton lies inside the background by construction, so that class scores 1.0 whatever the model did: measured on a 3-pixel vessel, averaging it in moved 0.7865 to 0.8933. It is not a flattering average, it is a number with no meaning in it.
include_background.title: Include Background

iterations.description: How many times the skeleton is peeled. It has to reach the half-width of the thickest structure or its core is never reduced to a centreline, and five covers a ten-pixel object. A retinal vessel is about nine pixels wide in the data - measured on FIVES as mask area over skeleton length, not the one to five often quoted, which is what a naive resize leaves behind - so five is enough for vessels and not much more than enough. Raise it for something thicker, at a cost linear in the number; too few is reported rather than scored, because an empty skeleton otherwise reads as a perfect 1.0.
iterations.title: Iterations

name.description: Centreline Dice, which measures whether a structure is connected rather than whether its pixels coincide. A skeleton is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run (`splits`) it is reported **per case** by `evaluate_cases`, which reassembles a case's tiles before measuring it. It is absent from the epoch and from the history there, because a per-batch average of a per-tile skeleton would be a number about nothing - which also means a callback cannot watch `val_cldice` on a tiled run, and the specification says so when it is read.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.
smooth.title: Smooth

ComboLoss.description:
A lopsided cross-entropy blended with Dice.

Two knobs that answer two different questions: `ce_ratio` tilts the cross-entropy
between punishing missed foreground and punishing false alarms, and `alpha` sets how
much of the total each half provides. Worth having when both the class imbalance and
the direction of the error matter; `cce_dice` is the simpler answer when only the
first does.

alpha.description: How much of the objective is the weighted cross-entropy term; the rest is Dice.
alpha.title: Alpha

ce_ratio.description: Within the cross-entropy term, how much weight goes on the positive class. This is the key that makes `combo` worth choosing over `cce_dice`: it lets the two halves of the objective disagree about which class matters.
ce_ratio.title: Ce Ratio

ConnectedComponents.description:
Label the thresholded foreground and ignore the separation signal entirely.

**The yardstick, and the reason it is compatible with every target.** It is what any
semantic model already gives for free, so a row of it beside the signal's own row is
what makes the signal's number readable: the same model, the same mask, the same
pictures, with and without the thing being measured. Everything else is 1 ms an image
against the 11 ms the others cost, so there is no reason to leave it out.

It is also a ceiling nothing can pass: touching objects are one region, so on the Data
Science Bowl's held-out cases a **perfect** semantic mask scores 0.7655 through this at
native size and 0.7505 at 256x256. A run that lands between the published weights'
0.4888 and that number has improved its mask and said nothing about separation.

```yaml
decode:
  - name: connected_components
```

minimum_area.description:
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.

It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.
minimum_area.title: Minimum Area

name.description: Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `follow_flows` takes `steps` and `step_size`, the others do not. A decoding the chosen `separation` cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.

CosineAnnealing.description:
Decay the learning rate along a cosine, from its initial value to `min_lr`.

No `monitor`: it is a function of how far through the run you are, not of how the run
is going. That is the difference from `reduce_lr_on_plateau`, and the two **cannot be
combined** - measured rather than assumed. A schedule recomputes the rate from the
optimiser's initial value at the end of every epoch, so it erases whatever the plateau
callback cut: with both configured the rate follows the cosine exactly, 0.0976, 0.0905,
0.0794 from 0.1, where the plateau alone reaches 1e-6 over the same six epochs. This
sentence used to say a run may want both, which was never true of the code.

epochs.description: How many epochs to spread the decay over. Unset means the model's `epochs`, which is what you want: a cosine that ends where the run ends. Setting it shorter parks the rate at `min_lr` for the remaining epochs, and longer stops the run part way down the curve.
epochs.title: Epochs

min_lr.description: The rate at the last epoch, which the cosine decays to from the optimiser's own learning_rate. Each parameter group decays from its own initial rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened at the first epoch - that would have been invisible, since the history records one learning_rate, the first group's.
min_lr.title: Min Lr

One member, and an enum anyway.

A `Literal["yolo3"]` would say the same thing today and would have to become an enum
the moment a second detector arrives, changing the type of a field the R package
sends. See `Architecture` for the same reasoning on the segmentation side.

DetectionData.description:
Where the images and their annotation files are.

`classes` is detection's answer to the colormap, and it is stated for the same reason:
the position of a name in this list *is* the class index the model learns. Read from
the annotation files instead, the order would come out alphabetical - reproducible,
and unrelated to anything. A model trained with `RBC` at index 0 and used where index
0 means `WBC` reports plausible boxes with plausible scores and nothing downstream can
tell.

Unlike a segmentation colormap there is no background entry. A pixel always belongs to
some class, so segmentation needs a name for "none of them"; a region of an image that
holds no object is simply not a box.

annotation_format.description: Pascal VOC XML, the format BCCD and most detection datasets ship, or LabelMe JSON. Both readers are in `pyplatypus.detection.annotations`.
annotation_format.title: Annotation Format

classes.description: Class names in class order. Position is the class index. No background entry - an image region with no object is not a box.
classes.title: Classes

column_sep.description: For `config_file`, what separates several paths inside one cell - a sample with one mask file per object, as Data Science Bowl has, or one file per channel.
column_sep.title: Column Sep

coordinates.description:
How to read a Pascal VOC box. The format's own convention is 1-based and inclusive of both endpoints, so a 10-pixel-wide box runs xmin=1 xmax=10 and the width is `xmax - xmin + 1`. Plenty of tools write the same files 0-based and exclusive, where that box is xmin=0 xmax=10. Reading one as the other shifts every box by a pixel and shrinks it by one, which is invisible at a glance and costs real IoU on small objects.
Unset means 'voc'. `describe_annotations` reports the evidence: a minimum coordinate of 0 proves the file is 0-based, since a 1-based index cannot be zero.
coordinates.title: Coordinates

mode.description: How the files are arranged: `nested_dirs` for one directory per sample, `config_file` for a CSV whose columns name the files. The CSV form is what to use when the data cannot be moved or copied into a layout.

shuffle.description: Shuffle the training data between epochs. Only the training data: validation is read in order so that two epochs measure the same thing in the same way.
shuffle.title: Shuffle

split.description: Divide `train_path` instead of naming a second folder. Nothing is written: the samples that were already discovered are partitioned, so a specification stays a description and leaves no files behind. `split_dataset()` is the tool when the CSVs are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, or to cite.

strict_labels.description: Refuse an object whose class is not in `classes`. False skips it instead, which is how you train on two of a dataset's three classes. True by default: an unexpected label is more often a typo in `classes` than an intention.
strict_labels.title: Strict Labels

subdirs.description: For `nested_dirs`, the two subdirectories of each sample directory: the images and the files holding their boxes. Which format those files are in is said by `annotation_format`, never guessed from the extension.
subdirs.title: Subdirs

test_path.description: A third set, scored only when asked. Whether it can be scored at all depends on whether it carries labels: a folder of images alone is accepted and `predict` works on it, while `evaluate` refuses it by name rather than failing two layers down on the first missing mask.
test_path.title: Test Path

train_path.description: Where the training data is. For `nested_dirs`, a directory of sample directories; for `config_file`, a CSV naming the files. With a `split`, this is the only path given and the divisions are cut from it.
train_path.title: Train Path

validation.description:
Whether this run validates at all. `false` is the third and last way of answering the question `validation_path` and `split` answer, and it has to be written down.

A final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled, is a legitimate thing to want - and until now it meant inventing a split and ignoring the number it produced. What is *not* legitimate is arriving here by omission: a specification with neither a path nor a split is still an error, because 'I have no validation set' and 'I forgot' look identical and only one of them is a decision.

With `false`, giving `validation_path` or `split` as well is refused: they say where the validation set comes from and this says there is not one.
validation.title: Validation

validation_path.description: Optional only in the sense that `split` is the other way to get one, and `validation: false` the third. Exactly one of them, because two sources for the validation set are two places to change it.
validation_path.title: Validation Path

window.description: How values in real units are mapped to 0-1: a named window such as 'lung' or 'soft_tissue', an explicit (centre, width) pair, 'auto' for the window the file recorded - DICOM only, since NIfTI stores none - or 'full' for the whole range present. A fixed window is what makes two scans comparable: scaling each one by its own extremes lets a single bright voxel rescale everything else. Ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255. Accepted as `dicom_window` too, the name it had while DICOM was the only format that needed it.
window.title: Window

DetectionData.title: DetectionData

DetectionModel.description:
One detector.

No `n_class`: the data's `classes` is the only place it is written. Segmentation
carries it on the model too and cross-checks the two, which is a consequence of its
history rather than a design - one source cannot disagree with itself.

anchors.description: The box shapes the model predicts offsets from, as fractions of the input size, one group per grid from coarsest to finest. Unset fits them to the training annotations with k-means under an IoU distance, which is what you want: measured on BCCD's 2,805 training boxes, COCO's anchors cover them at a mean IoU of 0.65 against 0.88 for anchors fitted to them. Fitted anchors are recorded with the run, since a detector cannot be reloaded without them.
anchors.title: Anchors

anchors_per_grid.description: How many anchors to fit per grid, when `anchors` is not given. It also sets the head's width, which is anchors_per_grid * (n_class + 5).
anchors_per_grid.title: Anchors Per Grid

architecture.description: Which detector. YOLOv3 is the only one, and it is 2D: boxes in a volume are a different problem with different annotations, so a detection specification at rank 3 is refused while the specification is read rather than failing later. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` names one, together with the anchors - weights mean nothing without the anchors they were trained with, so a specification naming both is refused.

augmentation.description: albumentations transforms, applied to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. Each step is probed at the model's own input size while the pipeline is built, because support for volumes is uneven and a transform that cannot take one raises from inside the library.
augmentation.title: Augmentation

batch_size.description: How many samples go through the network at once. Limited by memory rather than by the problem, and it is the first thing to lower when a 3D run will not fit. It interacts with `batch_normalization`: statistics taken over very few samples are noisy.
batch_size.title: Batch Size

box_loss.description:
How the box coordinates are scored. `offsets` is YOLOv3's own: cross-entropy on the two cell offsets and squared error on the two log sizes, each weighted by `2 - w*h` so a small object is not worth less than a large one. `giou` scores the decoded box against the true box directly, as `1 - GIoU`.

The reason to prefer `giou` is that **it can reach zero**. Cross-entropy against a soft target bottoms out at that target's entropy, so the `offsets` term is still 4.21 on a prediction that is exactly right - measured on three boxes - and a converged run cannot be told from a stalled one by reading it. The same prediction scores 0.000000 under `giou`.

**It is not the better objective here, and that is measured.** BCCD, three seeds each, 150 epochs, its own test split:

```
            mAP@0.5          mAP@COCO         matched IoU
giou        0.8666 +-0.0147  0.5078 +-0.0083  0.7929 +-0.0069
offsets     0.8583 +-0.0167  0.5172 +-0.0195  0.8038 +-0.0001
```

Average precision cannot separate them in either direction - both gaps are inside the noise. How well the matched boxes fit can, and `giou` is worse by 0.0109, which is 2.7 standard errors of the difference. It is also far less repeatable on exactly the quantity it targets: `offsets` gave 0.803853, 0.803656 and 0.803861 across its seeds, sixty times tighter than `giou`.

The reason is in the same run's own numbers. GIoU exists because IoU is a flat zero for boxes that do not touch, so it has no gradient where a detector is most wrong - but anchors fitted by k-means already cover BCCD's truths at a mean IoU of 0.877, so predictions never start disjoint and the advantage never arrives while the cost does. Where fitted anchors cover poorly it should be a different story, which is untested here and therefore not claimed.

So choose `giou` to make the objective **readable**, not to raise the score: at 150 epochs its coordinate term sits at 0.05 on the training split against 0.47 on validation, which is a localisation gap you can see, while `offsets` reads 5.92 and 6.85 against a floor of 5.891 and tells you nothing. On BCCD that legibility costs about 0.011 of matched IoU.
box_loss.title: Box Loss

callbacks.description: Things that happen between epochs: stopping early, writing checkpoints, moving the learning rate, averaging the weights. A callback watching a number no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever, and so is one watching `val_*` in a run with no validation set.
callbacks.title: Callbacks

channels.description: How many channels the network takes: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale, and one per sequence for multi-modal data such as the four MRI sequences in BraTS. Derived rather than declared when `channels_from` names the files, because then the data decides. Not adopted from a weights file - the data pipeline needs it before a network exists, and a specification has to be checkable offline.
channels.title: Channels

epochs.description: How many passes over the training data. The default is deliberately small: it is enough to see that a run works and not enough to mistake for a result. With `cosine_annealing` this is also the length the schedule is spread over.
epochs.title: Epochs

fit.description: Set false to load weights and skip training.
fit.title: Fit

ignore_threshold.description: A cell that is not responsible for an object but whose box overlaps one this much is left unsupervised rather than trained towards 'no object'. Without it a nearly-correct guess beside the responsible cell is punished, which is the one thing a detector should not learn.
ignore_threshold.title: Ignore Threshold

input_shape.description: Spatial size: (height, width) in 2D, (depth, height, width) in 3D.
input_shape.title: Input Shape

min_visibility.description:
How much of a box must survive an augmentation that removes part of the frame, as a fraction of its original area, for the box to be kept. A convention rather than a measurement; what is defensible is the direction. A box keeping two pixels of a cell teaches the model that a two-pixel fragment is a whole cell, which produces false positives everywhere, while dropping a heavily truncated object only fails to teach it about that object. Pascal VOC marks such objects `truncated` for the same reason.
Irrelevant unless a transform can lose part of the frame: flips and rotations never do.
min_visibility.title: Min Visibility

name.description: Unique within a spec; names the outputs.
name.title: Name

nms_threshold.description: Two boxes of the same class overlapping this much are one object, and the lower-scoring one is dropped. Per class, so a platelet sitting on a red cell survives.
nms_threshold.title: Nms Threshold

operating_point.description: The confidence at which precision and recall are reported. Separate from `score_threshold` because they answer different questions: that one decides what is computed at all, this one decides where on the curve to stand.
operating_point.title: Operating Point

optimizer.description: How the weights are updated. `name` selects which one and decides which other keys this block accepts.
optimizer.title: Optimizer

score_threshold.description: Discard a predicted box below this confidence. Low on purpose: average precision is computed over the whole ranking, so a cut here is a ceiling on recall that no threshold chosen later can lift.
score_threshold.title: Score Threshold

weights.description: Registry name (e.g. 'dsbowl-unet') or a path to a local checkpoint.
weights.title: Weights

DetectionModel.title: DetectionModel

data.description: Where the images and their annotations are, and how to read them.

deterministic.description:
Ask torch for deterministic algorithms as well, which is the only thing that makes a run on a card repeatable - `seed` alone does not, and the field above says so.

**It is an opt-in because the cost is real and arrives late.** Some convolutions become much slower, and an operation that has no deterministic implementation raises *when it is reached* - so a run can stop ten minutes in rather than when the specification was checked. Every other refusal here happens before anything is read; this one cannot, because whether an operation has a deterministic algorithm is a fact about the installed torch and the device, not about the configuration.

Needs `seed`: constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies produces a run that is no more repeatable and only slower, so asking for it without a seed is refused rather than quietly accepted.
deterministic.title: Deterministic

models.description: One or more detectors, trained in turn against the same data. Names must be unique, for the same reason as in a segmentation specification.
models.title: Models

output_dir.description: Where a run record is written, and where `fit()` puts anything it is asked to save. Nothing is written unless something asks to write: naming this does not by itself create a directory.
output_dir.title: Output Dir

seed.description:
Makes a run repeatable as far as the arithmetic is deterministic, which goes further on some hardware than others - so it is worth knowing where it stops.

**Repeatable:** the split (`split_dataset` gives the same partition on any machine), a detector's fitted anchors, the order the data arrives in and its augmentation - including inside the loader's worker processes - and, on the processor, every number to twelve decimal places.

**Not repeatable:** a run on a CUDA device. Measured on a GTX 1070: two runs at one seed agreed to twelve decimals on the processor and differed in the fourth after a single epoch on the card, because cuDNN chooses algorithms this does not constrain. Nor across versions of this package - anything that changes the order data is drawn in changes what one seed draws, and `0.8.0a3` did exactly that.

So it is the field for comparing two of your own runs, and not for publishing a number somebody else can land on.
seed.title: Seed

DiceLoss.description:
Overlap, and nothing about where the error sits.

The one to reach for first on a single foreground class. It counts a wrong voxel the
same whether it sits in the middle of the object or a long way outside it, which is
`boundary`'s whole reason for existing, and on a small object a single missed piece
moves it a lot. `smooth` is what keeps it from 0/0 on an empty mask.

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.
smooth.title: Smooth

DiceLoss.title: DiceLoss

DiceMetric.description:
The number to report unless there is a reason not to.

Scored on the mask rather than on the objective, so a Dice-trained and a focal-trained
model are comparable. It ranks models identically to `iou`, so reporting both is one
result twice; `smooth` and `include_background` are what make it flatter or honest.

include_background.description: Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.
include_background.title: Include Background

name.description: Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.
smooth.title: Smooth

DiceMetric.title: DiceMetric

EarlyStopping.description:
Stop when the watched number stops improving, and keep the weights that did.

What it buys is the epochs after the best one, which on a long run is most of the wall
clock. The failure to watch for is stopping on noise: where the monitored number
wanders, `patience` alone is not enough and `min_delta` is what makes an improvement
count. `restore_best` is on, because the last weights are by definition the ones that
were not improving.

min_delta.description: Improvement smaller than this does not count as improvement. Useful where the watched number wanders: without it, noise alone keeps resetting the patience.
min_delta.title: Min Delta

monitor.description: What to watch: `val_loss`, `train_loss`, or `val_` followed by a metric the model asks for, such as `val_dice`. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in `loss` is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching `val_*` in a run with `validation: false`, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.
monitor.title: Monitor

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

patience.description: Epochs to wait, with no improvement, before acting.
patience.title: Patience

restore_best.description: Put the best weights back when training stops, rather than keeping the last - which are by definition the ones that were not improving. Note that `swa` replaces nothing if a run stops before averaging began.
restore_best.title: Restore Best

start.description:
Do not act before this fraction of the run has passed - 0.1 leaves the first tenth alone. Mutually exclusive with `start_epoch`: a fraction survives a change to `epochs` and an epoch count does not. Unset is no warm-up, which is what this callback did before `0.8.0a34`.

**It delays the stopping and nothing else.** An epoch before the warm-up ends can still become the best one and `restore_best` can still return to it - those weights are the best the run has if it ends for some other reason, and throwing them away to tidy the bookkeeping would lose a real answer.
start.title: Start

start_epoch.description: Do not act before this epoch, 1-based. Mutually exclusive with `start`. This is the one to use when the warm-up is a property of the optimisation rather than of the run's length - a schedule's warm-up is fifteen epochs whether the run is 60 or 600.
start_epoch.title: Start Epoch

EarlyStopping.title: EarlyStopping

Ema.description:
An exponential moving average of the weights, updated every optimiser step.

`swa`'s sibling and the other answer to the same observation: the last epoch's corner
is not the middle of the basin. `swa` averages the tail uniformly from a declared
start; this weights recent weights more and needs no start at all, because an average
with a decay forgets the beginning by itself.

**Updated per step, which is what makes it the estimator the literature means.** A
decay of 0.999 is 0.999 per *step*: over 60 epochs of 200 batches that is 12,000
updates and a half-life of about 700 steps. Announced per epoch the same number would
do almost nothing, and offering it that way would have been publishing a name whose
documented values mean something else - which is why `0.8.0a37` added a fourth
callback hook rather than approximating one.

Buffers are averaged too, which is the difference from `swa`: there a pass over the
training data recomputes batch-normalisation statistics at the end, because a uniform
average of weights has no matching statistics. An exponential average that also
averages the buffers carries its own, so it needs no second pass over the data.

One averager per run: `ema` and `swa` together are refused rather than silently
applied in the order the list happened to have them.

decay.description: How much of the average survives each step. 0.999 is the usual value and means a half-life of about 700 steps - roughly three and a half epochs at 200 batches each. **Per step, not per epoch**, so the published values transfer: a run with few steps wants a smaller number, because an average that forgets more slowly than the run is long never leaves its starting point. The model is replaced by the average when training ends.
decay.title: Decay

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

Ema.title: Ema

Flows.description:
A unit vector field pointing at each object's sink, plus the semantic channels.

Two continuous channels in front of the classes, and **no pixel spent on being a
boundary** - which is the structural argument for it, and the reason it was built after
`rim` closed measured-and-no. It makes the objective composite and the activation
partial: the vectors stay as the network produced them while the classes are softmaxed,
and `InstanceObjective` is where those two halves meet. `Separation.FLOWS` has what it
turned out to be worth.

```yaml
separation:
  name: flows
  mode: diffusion
  loss:
    name: smooth_l1
    where: foreground
  weight: 1.0
```

loss.description:
The objective on the two vector channels, which is a different question from the model's own `loss` - that one scores the mask. A continuous target has nothing in the overlap-and-cross-entropy losses to be trained against, so this is one of `mse`, `l1` or `smooth_l1`, and anything else is refused by name: `loss: dice` against a vector field would return a number and a gradient, which is the worst available outcome.

Left unset it is `mse` with `where: foreground`, which is what the measured run used. `where` is the field to read before changing it, because the foreground is 13.97% of a Data Science Bowl image and `everywhere` spends 86% of the objective on a background zero.
loss.title: Loss

mode.description:
How the vector field is built: towards each object's centroid in a straight line, or down the gradient of heat diffused inside it.

**`diffusion` is the default because the two were measured on the ground truth before anything was trained**: decoded back into objects they reach 0.9924 and 0.9478. The obvious explanation for the gap is not the cause - only 19 of 6000 objects have their centroid outside themselves, 0.32% - and the real one is one level down: a straight line between two pixels of a discrete set can leave the set even when the object looks convex, which splits an object whose own centroid is inside it.

`centroid` is 23 times cheaper to build (4.9 ms a case against 113.6 ms), which is the reason to reach for it and is small beside an epoch.
mode.title: Mode

name.description:
Which separation signal, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `rim` takes `width`, `flows` takes `mode`, `loss` and `weight`. A setting that belongs to the other mechanism is not refused here, it is **unwritable** - `width` under `name: flows` is an unknown key, which is the answer every typo in a specification gets.

That is this block's reason to be a block, and it was built flat first: `separation: rim` beside `rim_width`, `flow_mode`, `flow_loss` and `flow_weight`. The flat form parses, so it needs a validator and a table of which field belongs to which mechanism to refuse half of what it accepts, and it shows every reader four fields of which two can apply to them. This form shows a reader of `name: rim` one field, and the refusal is gone rather than written - `extra="forbid"` was already doing that job for every other key in the file.
name.title: Name

weight.description: How much the vector term counts against the mask term, which are summed. The default is 1.0 and it is measured rather than conventional: on the 60-epoch run the two terms are the same order of magnitude throughout - 0.5937 against 0.6345 after the first epoch and 0.0734 against 0.0659 at the last - so neither half of the objective is drowning the other at this weight.
weight.title: Weight

Flows.title: Flows

FocalLoss.description:
Cross-entropy that loses interest in the voxels it already gets right.

`gamma` is the whole feature: at 0 this is exactly cross-entropy - measured, the two
agree to floating point - and raising it pushes the loss onto the hard voxels. Worth
having where the easy background dominates the gradient. The cost is that a model that
is right but unconfident everywhere is barely trained at all.

alpha.description: Weight on the positive class, between 0 and 1. Unset means no weighting, which is not the same as 0.5: at 0.5 both classes are halved and the gradients are smaller, which looks like a learning-rate change.
alpha.title: Alpha

gamma.description: How hard to discount the pixels already classified well, so the gradient comes from the ones that are not. 0 is plain cross-entropy; 2 is the usual value.
gamma.title: Gamma

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

FocalLoss.title: FocalLoss

FocalTverskyLoss.description:
Tversky, with the same loss of interest in what is already right.

`gamma` raises `1 - TI` to a power, so the cases near the truth stop contributing. At
`gamma = 1` this is exactly the Tversky loss - measured - so like `focal`, the
parameter *is* the feature. Reach for it when the asymmetry of `tversky` is wanted and
a majority of easy cases is drowning it.

alpha.description: Weight on false negatives, as in `tversky`, with false positives taking 1 - alpha.
alpha.title: Alpha

gamma.description: Exponent on the Tversky index, which is where this differs from `tversky`: above 1 it concentrates the gradient on the cases scoring badly. Note 1 is the default and means plain Tversky, not 'off'.
gamma.title: Gamma

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.
smooth.title: Smooth

FocalTverskyLoss.title: FocalTverskyLoss

FollowFlows.description:
Follow the field from every foreground pixel and label the basins they arrive in.

**No seed, no interior, nothing eroded**, which is the point of the flow target: pixels
that arrive at the same place are one object, and the places are found rather than
assumed. The highest ceiling of the four on perfect parts, 0.9873.

minimum_area.description:
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.

It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.
minimum_area.title: Minimum Area

name.description: Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `follow_flows` takes `steps` and `step_size`, the others do not. A decoding the chosen `separation` cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.
name.title: Name

step_size.description: How far one step moves, in pixels, on a unit-length field. **This one is a cliff**: 0.9923 at 1.0, 0.4715 at 2.0, 0.0303 at 10.0. A step longer than a pixel jumps over the sink it was converging on and lands in a neighbour's basin, so this is not a speed knob - raise it and the decoding stops working.
step_size.title: Step Size

steps.description: How many Euler steps each pixel takes. **Measured as not mattering**: one step scores 0.9914 against 0.9923 converged, a span below the 0.0013 two runs differ by. The field is continuous, so one object's pixels stay together, and it diverges at a seam, so the gap between two objects opens on the first step rather than after many. Left adjustable because that argument is about this data's object sizes, and lowering it is the cheap thing to try on larger ones.
steps.title: Steps

FollowFlows.title: FollowFlows

GeneralizedDiceLoss.description:
Dice with every class weighted by the inverse square of how much of the picture it
occupies, so a rare class counts for more than an equal share rather than for less.

**The usual argument for this loss does not apply here and is not made.** It is
normally introduced as a fix for Dice being dominated by the background; `dice` in this
package is a mean over the class channels, so a lesion in 1% of the frame already
carries the same weight as the 99% around it. Measured on a 1% target with two
predictions - one finding the lesion and leaking a false positive of equal size, one
missing it entirely and getting the background perfect:

    dice               0.1658 finding   0.4731 missing   prefers finding by 0.3073
    cce                0.1600 finding   0.1600 missing   indifferent
    cce_dice           0.1629 finding   0.3166 missing   prefers finding by 0.1536
    generalized_dice   0.3278 finding   0.9511 missing   prefers finding by 0.6233

So what this adds is weight **beyond** an equal share: on that target the classes are
weighted 1 to 9801 rather than 1 to 1, and the margin between finding the lesion and
missing it doubles. And the objective that is genuinely dominated is the per-pixel half
of `cce_dice`: to `cce` a false positive and a missed lesion of the same size are the
same number of wrong pixels, which is the indifference in that table.

**The run that motivates it is in this project's record and the loss was never the
variable.** On SIIM-ACR pneumothorax, a median 0.59% of the frame, the built-in encoder
scored `0.0531 +/- 0.0586` over three seeds - a spread larger than its own mean, with
two of three seeds never learning at all - and every arm of that table used `cce_dice`.

**Not a third `tversky`.** `tversky` moves the balance between false positives and
false negatives by a number you choose; `focal_tversky` reweights hard examples. This
reweights **classes by how much of the image they occupy**, computed from the batch
rather than set by hand. Three losses, three questions, and a reader who picks by name
will pick wrongly.

Two things to know before reaching for it. With every class the same size it is
**exactly `dice` pooled over the classes** - a test rather than a claim - so it costs
nothing and buys nothing on a balanced problem. And the weights are recomputed per
batch, so a batch holding no lesion at all is scored on flat weights; with `batch_size`
1 on a sparse dataset that is most batches, which is an argument for a larger batch
rather than against the loss.

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.
smooth.title: Smooth

InstanceData.description:
Where the images and their per-object masks are.

**The one thing this says that a semantic data block cannot**: the masks are read one
file per object and keep their identity. `unite_masks()` is what the semantic pipeline
does with the same files, and its own docstring says the cost - the element-wise maximum
merges them, so instance identity is gone at read time. Nothing new has to be collected
to train or score instances on the Data Science Bowl, which ships 670 cases of exactly
this shape; it only has to be read differently.

There is no `colormap`, no `labels` and no `regions` here, because none of them is how
this data names anything: a directory of per-object files says where the objects are and
says nothing about what kind they are. `n_class` is therefore 2 and derived rather than
declared - see the property.

column_sep.description: For `config_file`, what separates several paths inside one cell - a sample with one mask file per object, as Data Science Bowl has, or one file per channel.
column_sep.title: Column Sep

mode.description: How the files are arranged: `nested_dirs` for one directory per sample, `config_file` for a CSV whose columns name the files. The CSV form is what to use when the data cannot be moved or copied into a layout.

shuffle.description: Shuffle the training data between epochs. Only the training data: validation is read in order so that two epochs measure the same thing in the same way.
shuffle.title: Shuffle

split.description: Divide `train_path` instead of naming a second folder. Nothing is written: the samples that were already discovered are partitioned, so a specification stays a description and leaves no files behind. `split_dataset()` is the tool when the CSVs are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, or to cite.

subdirs.description: For `nested_dirs`, the two subdirectories of each sample directory: the images, and **one mask file per object**. A case with 375 nuclei has 375 files here, which is the Data Science Bowl's own layout; they are read as a label map with one value per object rather than united into one mask, which is the whole difference between this task and `semantic_segmentation`.
subdirs.title: Subdirs

test_path.description: A third set, scored only when asked. Whether it can be scored at all depends on whether it carries labels: a folder of images alone is accepted and `predict` works on it, while `evaluate` refuses it by name rather than failing two layers down on the first missing mask.
test_path.title: Test Path

train_path.description: Where the training data is. For `nested_dirs`, a directory of sample directories; for `config_file`, a CSV naming the files. With a `split`, this is the only path given and the divisions are cut from it.
train_path.title: Train Path

validation.description:
Whether this run validates at all. `false` is the third and last way of answering the question `validation_path` and `split` answer, and it has to be written down.

A final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled, is a legitimate thing to want - and until now it meant inventing a split and ignoring the number it produced. What is *not* legitimate is arriving here by omission: a specification with neither a path nor a split is still an error, because 'I have no validation set' and 'I forgot' look identical and only one of them is a decision.

With `false`, giving `validation_path` or `split` as well is refused: they say where the validation set comes from and this says there is not one.
validation.title: Validation

validation_path.description: Optional only in the sense that `split` is the other way to get one, and `validation: false` the third. Exactly one of them, because two sources for the validation set are two places to change it.
validation_path.title: Validation Path

window.description: How values in real units are mapped to 0-1: a named window such as 'lung' or 'soft_tissue', an explicit (centre, width) pair, 'auto' for the window the file recorded - DICOM only, since NIfTI stores none - or 'full' for the whole range present. A fixed window is what makes two scans comparable: scaling each one by its own extremes lets a single bright voxel rescale everything else. Ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255. Accepted as `dicom_window` too, the name it had while DICOM was the only format that needed it.
window.title: Window

InstanceData.title: InstanceData

InstanceModel.description:
One instance model: a U-shaped network, a separation target, and how to decode it.

Everything a semantic model has, plus the two axes. `loss` and `metrics` keep their
meaning and apply to the **semantic channels** - the mask - which is why the first
number any of these runs reports is foreground Dice: if the mask moved, the instance
number moved for a reason that is not separation, and nothing else in the table can
tell those apart.

activation.description: The non-linearity between convolutions, the same one throughout.

architecture.description: Which U-shaped network. Measured on Data Science Bowl, one split, 60 epochs, the four span 0.9187 to 0.9217 of Dice - a spread of 0.0030, against 0.054 between images within any one of them, and 0.0012 from re-running one of them with another seed. On that problem the architecture is not where the result comes from. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` names one.

augmentation.description: albumentations transforms, applied to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. Each step is probed at the model's own input size while the pipeline is built, because support for volumes is uneven and a transform that cannot take one raises from inside the library.
augmentation.title: Augmentation

batch_normalization.description: Normalise between convolutions. On by default, and worth knowing about when weights are averaged: `swa` has to recompute these statistics over the training data, because an averaged weight tensor inherits them from whichever epoch was last rather than averaging them.
batch_normalization.title: Batch Normalization

batch_size.description: How many samples go through the network at once. Limited by memory rather than by the problem, and it is the first thing to lower when a 3D run will not fit. It interacts with `batch_normalization`: statistics taken over very few samples are noisy.
batch_size.title: Batch Size

block_width.description: Convolutions per block, at every level. 2 is what every U-Net paper uses and what the published weights were trained with; raising it adds depth without adding levels, which is the lever to reach for when the objects are small enough that halving the resolution again would lose them.
block_width.title: Block Width

blocks.description: How many times the resolution is halved, so how much context the deepest layer sees. `input_shape` must divide by 2^blocks. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` is given and this is not; with an `encoder`, the backbone's own depth is the ceiling.
blocks.title: Blocks

callbacks.description: Things that happen between epochs: stopping early, writing checkpoints, moving the learning rate, averaging the weights. A callback watching a number no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever, and so is one watching `val_*` in a run with no validation set.
callbacks.title: Callbacks

channels.description: How many channels the network takes: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale, and one per sequence for multi-modal data such as the four MRI sequences in BraTS. Derived rather than declared when `channels_from` names the files, because then the data decides. Not adopted from a weights file - the data pipeline needs it before a network exists, and a specification has to be checkable offline.
channels.title: Channels

decode.description:
How the predicted channels become objects. **A list**, because several decodings share one forward pass: a second decoding of 134 images costs 1.41 s against 16 minutes for a second training run, so this is `metrics:` rather than `callbacks:` - `evaluate()` returns one row per (model, decoding).

Each entry is a block with a `name` and that decoding's own parameters. A decoding the `separation` cannot feed - `follow_flows` with `rim`, say - is refused at load time with both halves named, rather than returning a label map of something else.

**Left unset it is the signal's own decoding plus `connected_components`**, which is the pair that makes a row readable: the same model and the same mask with and without the separation signal. Write the list to choose; leave it out and the comparison every one of these runs needs is already there.

With `splits`, decoding happens after the tiles are stitched, never per tile - an object crossing a seam would otherwise become two objects, and that is a constraint of the task rather than a setting.
decode.title: Decode

deep_supervision.description: Train every decoder depth rather than only the last, each at input resolution. `u_net_plus_plus` only, since it is the architecture with intermediate outputs to supervise.
deep_supervision.title: Deep Supervision

dropout.description: Drop this fraction during training. 0 switches it off, which is the default because these models are small enough that batch normalisation usually carries the regularisation on its own.
dropout.title: Dropout

encoder.description: A timm backbone to use as the contracting path, e.g. 'resnet34'. Leave unset for the built-in encoder, which is the only one that works in 3D.
encoder.title: Encoder

encoder_learning_rate.description: A separate, usually smaller learning rate for the layers that arrived pretrained. Whatever is ours trains at the optimizer's own rate instead - the decoder and the full-resolution stage in front of the backbone for a segmentation model, the pooled head for a classifier - because those start random. Unset means one rate for the whole network.
encoder_learning_rate.title: Encoder Learning Rate

epochs.description: How many passes over the training data. The default is deliberately small: it is enough to see that a run works and not enough to mistake for a result. With `cosine_annealing` this is also the length the schedule is spread over.
epochs.title: Epochs

filters.description: Filters in the first block, doubled at every level, so this sets the model's size more than anything else does. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` is given and this is not.
filters.title: Filters

fit.description: Set false to load weights and skip training.
fit.title: Fit

freeze_encoder.description: Keep the pretrained layers fixed for this many epochs, then train them. Lets the random part of the network settle - the decoder, or a classifier's head - before its gradients reach weights worth keeping. A number at or above `epochs` freezes them for the whole run.
freeze_encoder.title: Freeze Encoder

initialiser.description: How the weights start. The `he_*` family is scaled for ReLU-like activations and `glorot_*` for symmetric ones, so this and `activation` are a pair.

input_shape.description: Spatial size: (height, width) in 2D, (depth, height, width) in 3D.
input_shape.title: Input Shape

loss.description: The objective trained against. The `loss` column of a score table is comparable only between models trained on the same one - a Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a cross-entropy of 0.14, it is not the same question - which is why the table carries the loss's name beside it.
loss.title: Loss

metrics.description: What to report beside the loss, computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so these stay comparable across models. A callback watching `val_<metric>` is refused when nothing here will produce it.
metrics.title: Metrics

name.description: Unique within a spec; names the outputs.
name.title: Name

optimizer.description: How the weights are updated. `name` selects which one and decides which other keys this block accepts.
optimizer.title: Optimizer

pretrained.description: Load the encoder's ImageNet weights. Separate from `encoder` on purpose: naming a backbone builds that architecture, and this is the flag that reaches the network, which matters where there is no network.
pretrained.title: Pretrained

separable_conv.description: Depthwise-separable convolutions: far fewer parameters for the same shape, and a little slower to converge.
separable_conv.title: Separable Conv

separation.description:
What the network predicts so that one mask can become many objects: a block named `rim` or `flows`, carrying that mechanism's own settings. **Required unless `weights` names a file that records what it was trained to predict**, because it decides the width of the head and which losses are admissible - the two things a model cannot be built without - and because neither value is a safe guess at what somebody meant.

A published file is the one place it does not have to be guessed. `dsbowl-instances` records `rim` at width 2, so leaving this out beside `weights: dsbowl-instances` adopts a training decision rather than inventing one, and the engine prints what it took. It was required outright until `0.8.0a28`, which left four of this model's fields as the file's own fingerprint with no way to learn them but a model card - and `separation` is the one nobody can guess, since a rim's width is not a shape. `pyplatypus#236`.

A block rather than a bare name because the settings differ between the two and belong inside the one they describe: `width` under `name: flows` is an unknown key rather than something a validator has to refuse.

It is also the field whose documentation carries a result: on the Data Science Bowl the two are worth +0.0640 and +0.0680 of instance average precision over the same mask through `connected_components`, a difference below the noise between two runs of one configuration, while a perfect mask is worth +0.2398. Read the blocks' own descriptions for what that means before planning a comparison around this axis.
separation.title: Separation

spatial_dropout.description: Drop whole feature maps rather than individual activations. The right kind for images, because neighbouring pixels in one map are correlated and dropping them one at a time removes less than it appears to. Has no effect unless `dropout` is above 0.
spatial_dropout.title: Spatial Dropout

splits.description: Cut each image into a grid of tiles instead of shrinking it. One entry per spatial dimension, e.g. [2, 3] cuts into 2 rows by 3 columns. The source is read at splits * input_shape and divided; every tile is input_shape. Leave unset to resize the whole image instead. Training then shuffles in windows rather than over every tile, so one decode serves all of a sample's tiles: measured on 2048-pixel retinas cut sixteen ways, the loader costs 254 ms a tile shuffled wholesale against 49 ms this way, and a batch still draws from several sources.
splits.title: Splits

weights.description: Registry name (e.g. 'dsbowl-unet') or a path to a local checkpoint.
weights.title: Weights

InstanceModel.title: InstanceModel

InstanceSpec.description:
Objects rather than classes: which object every pixel belongs to, scored as instances.

The same images and the same U-shaped networks as `semantic_segmentation`, with the
masks read one file per object instead of united into one. Two fields are new on a
model - `separation`, what the network predicts, and `decode`, a list of ways to turn
those channels into objects - and `pyplatypus.spec.instances` is where both are
documented, measurements included.

**What this task is honestly worth, said here because the tag's name promises more.**
A reader who writes `task: instance_segmentation` gets a semantic model with a
separation target, decoded into objects and scored by the Data Science Bowl's own
average precision. On that dataset the separation signal is worth +0.068 at best while
a perfect mask is worth +0.2398, so the limit is the mask rather than the separation -
and `connected_components`, which ignores the signal entirely, is always available as
the row every other row is read against. The capability is real, the ceiling is
measured, and both are in the documentation rather than in a footnote.

data.description: Where the images and their per-object masks are, and how to read them.

deterministic.description:
Ask torch for deterministic algorithms as well, which is the only thing that makes a run on a card repeatable - `seed` alone does not, and the field above says so.

**It is an opt-in because the cost is real and arrives late.** Some convolutions become much slower, and an operation that has no deterministic implementation raises *when it is reached* - so a run can stop ten minutes in rather than when the specification was checked. Every other refusal here happens before anything is read; this one cannot, because whether an operation has a deterministic algorithm is a fact about the installed torch and the device, not about the configuration.

Needs `seed`: constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies produces a run that is no more repeatable and only slower, so asking for it without a seed is refused rather than quietly accepted.
deterministic.title: Deterministic

models.description: One or more models, trained in turn against the same data. Names must be unique, for the same reason as in a segmentation specification. Several entries differing only in `separation` is the comparison this task exists to make easy - and `decode` widens the table again without a second run.
models.title: Models

output_dir.description: Where a run record is written, and where `fit()` puts anything it is asked to save. Nothing is written unless something asks to write: naming this does not by itself create a directory.
output_dir.title: Output Dir

seed.description:
Makes a run repeatable as far as the arithmetic is deterministic, which goes further on some hardware than others - so it is worth knowing where it stops.

**Repeatable:** the split (`split_dataset` gives the same partition on any machine), a detector's fitted anchors, the order the data arrives in and its augmentation - including inside the loader's worker processes - and, on the processor, every number to twelve decimal places.

**Not repeatable:** a run on a CUDA device. Measured on a GTX 1070: two runs at one seed agreed to twelve decimals on the processor and differed in the fourth after a single epoch on the card, because cuDNN chooses algorithms this does not constrain. Nor across versions of this package - anything that changes the order data is drawn in changes what one seed draws, and `0.8.0a3` did exactly that.

So it is the field for comparing two of your own runs, and not for publishing a number somebody else can land on.
seed.title: Seed

InstanceSpec.title: InstanceSpec

IouLoss.description:
Dice's harsher twin: the same ordering, a lower number.

Without smoothing the coefficient is exactly `dice / (2 - dice)`, which is strictly
increasing - measured here over twelve predictions, the two rank them identically. So
the choice is about which number you want to read, not which model you get. As a loss
the gradients still differ, and whether that changes a trained model is not measured.

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.
smooth.title: Smooth

IouLoss.title: IouLoss

IouMetric.description:
The same ordering as Dice, on the scale papers outside medicine use.

Without smoothing it is exactly `dice / (2 - dice)`, measured here, so it adds no
information to a report that already carries Dice - it is the convention of the
audience rather than a second opinion.

include_background.description: Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.
include_background.title: Include Background

name.description: Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.
smooth.title: Smooth

IouMetric.title: IouMetric

L1Loss.description:
Absolute error on a continuous target.

The same gradient however wrong the voxel is, which makes it robust to a handful of bad
labels and indifferent to being nearly right. Reach for it where the target has
outliers you do not want the model chasing.

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

where.description:
Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.

A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is **13.97% of the pixels at 256x256** (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so `everywhere` spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.

`foreground` divides by the mask's own total, which makes the number mean *average error per object voxel*. `everywhere` is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net's plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; `foreground` is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.

`foreground` asks the loader for the mask, which is the same mechanism `boundary` uses for its distance map. It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object's centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (`pyplatypus#211`).
where.title: Where

L1Loss.title: L1Loss

LinearAnnealing.description:
Decay the learning rate in a straight line, from its initial value to `min_lr`.

`cosine_annealing`'s simpler sibling and the same shape of argument: a function of how
far through the run you are rather than of how the run is going. A straight line spends
longer at high rates than a cosine does at the start and less at the end, which is the
whole difference; which one is better is a property of the problem and not a thing this
package has measured.

Like every schedule here, it is exclusive with the other schedules and with
`reduce_lr_on_plateau`.

epochs.description: How many epochs to spread the decay over. Unset means the model's `epochs`, which is what you want: a line that reaches `min_lr` where the run ends. Setting it shorter parks the rate at `min_lr` for the remaining epochs.
epochs.title: Epochs

min_lr.description: The rate at the last epoch, which the line descends to from the optimiser's own learning_rate. Each parameter group descends from its own initial rate, so an encoder_learning_rate is not flattened at the first epoch.
min_lr.title: Min Lr

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

LinearAnnealing.title: LinearAnnealing

LovaszLoss.description:
Optimise the overlap you are going to report, rather than a proxy for it.

A surrogate for the Jaccard index that is differentiable without being smoothed, so it
acts directly on the quantity `iou` is scored by. It sorts the errors of every image it
is given, which costs more than the elementwise losses, and `per_image` decides whether
that happens per image or over the batch: per image is the harsher reading and on mostly
empty images it is also the noisier one.

**Mutually exclusive classes only.** The Lovasz-Softmax surrogate sorts the errors of a
softmax over classes that are alternatives and walks the Lovasz extension of the Jaccard
loss along that order. The independent form is the Lovasz-Hinge, a different construction
over signed margins rather than a setting on this one - so `regions` is refused here
rather than silently served, because run on sigmoid channels this would return a number
and a gradient, which is the worst available outcome.

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

per_image.description: Compute the loss for each image and average, rather than over the whole batch at once. Per image is the honest thing when images differ in how much of them is foreground, because otherwise a large object in one image dominates the batch; it is also noisier.
per_image.title: Per Image

LovaszLoss.title: LovaszLoss

ModelCheckpoint.description:
The run's safety net - one file, overwritten.

Not a history and not a publication: `export_weights()` is what writes a file somebody
else can load, with a sidecar saying what it is. Use this so an interrupted run is not
a lost run, and `save_best_only: false` when interruption rather than the best epoch is
what you are guarding against.

monitor.description: What to watch: `val_loss`, `train_loss`, or `val_` followed by a metric the model asks for, such as `val_dice`. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in `loss` is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching `val_*` in a run with `validation: false`, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.
monitor.title: Monitor

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

path.description: Where to write the checkpoint. One file, overwritten - this is the run's safety net, not a history; `export_weights()` is what produces a file to publish, with a sidecar recording what it is. **The extension decides the format**: `.safetensors` is written as safetensors and anything else as a torch archive, which is what `.pt` has always meant here. Reading does not depend on the name - both formats are recognised by their contents - so a file written by an older version still loads under whatever it was called.
path.title: Path

save_best_only.description: Write only when the watched number improves. With `false` every epoch is written, which is what to use when a run may be interrupted rather than when the best epoch is wanted.
save_best_only.title: Save Best Only

when.description:
Thresholds that must all hold before anything is written: `{val_dice: 0.9, val_loss: 0.2}` writes nothing until the model is at least that good. Each key is a quantity this model reports, checked when the specification is built rather than at the first epoch.

**The direction is derived, not configured.** Anything ending in `loss` has to be *below* its threshold and everything else *above* it, which is the same rule `monitor` already uses - so there is no `above`/`below` to get backwards.

**This is an extra gate, not a replacement for `save_best_only`.** With both, a file is written when the watched number improves *and* every threshold holds.

**A threshold is a number about your data.** Unlike `patience` or `factor` it does not transfer: `val_dice: 0.9` copied from somebody else's configuration means something entirely different on other images. And a run whose conditions never hold writes nothing at all - the callback says so when the run ends, rather than leaving an empty directory to be discovered later.
when.title: When

ModelCheckpoint.title: ModelCheckpoint

MseLoss.description:
Squared error on a continuous target.

For `flows` and `hv`, and for nothing a mask can do: run against a one-hot target this
scores raw output against 0 and 1 with no activation in between, which is not a
segmentation objective. The gradient grows with the error, so one badly wrong voxel
counts for a lot - right when the large values of the target are the informative ones,
wrong when the labels are noisy.

```yaml
loss:
  name: mse
  where: foreground
```

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.

A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. `foreground` divides by the mask's own total, which makes the number mean *average error per object voxel*. `everywhere` is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net's plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; `foreground` is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.

`foreground` asks the loader for the mask, which is the same mechanism `boundary` uses for its distance map. It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object's centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (`pyplatypus#211`).
