NAdam.description:
Adam with the look-ahead that `sgd` calls `nesterov`.

The momentum term is applied before the gradient is measured rather than after. It
tends to move faster in the first epochs and to land in the same place; worth trying
where a run is slow to leave its initialisation.

beta_1.description: Decay for the running average of the gradient. Lower reacts to the last few batches, higher smooths over more of them; 0.9 is the usual value and rarely worth moving.
beta_1.title: Beta 1

beta_2.description: Decay for the running average of the squared gradient, which is what scales each parameter's step. Lowering it below about 0.99 makes training noticeably noisier.
beta_2.title: Beta 2

eps.description: Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.
eps.title: Eps

learning_rate.description: How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an `encoder_learning_rate` is not flattened by a schedule.
learning_rate.title: Learning Rate

name.description: Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `sgd` takes `momentum`, the Adam family takes `beta_1` and `beta_2`. `learning_rate` and `weight_decay` are accepted by all of them.
name.title: Name

weight_decay.description: Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.
weight_decay.title: Weight Decay

NAdam.title: NAdam

NearestSeed.description:
Grow the predicted interiors outward: every other foreground pixel joins the nearest.

A Voronoi partition of the foreground around the interiors, which one distance
transform answers. Not a watershed: it splits on distance alone, so the join lands on
the geometric midline wherever the picture says the objects part. For nuclei - small,
roughly convex, meeting along a short seam - the two agree closely.

**The better of the two rim decodings, measured**: 0.5561 against the watershed's
0.5458 on one trained model, and 0.9846 against 0.9703 on the ground truth. A
foreground pixel no seed can reach stays background rather than becoming an object of
its own, which is the honest answer when the model said "object here" and "no centre
anywhere".

minimum_area.description:
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.

It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.
minimum_area.title: Minimum Area

name.description: Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `follow_flows` takes `steps` and `step_size`, the others do not. A decoding the chosen `separation` cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.
name.title: Name

NearestSeed.title: NearestSeed

ReduceLrOnPlateau.description:
Cut the learning rate when the evidence says the run has stalled.

The difference from `cosine_annealing` is that this one reacts rather than follows a
schedule, so it may never fire at all - which is why a cosine beside `swa` is refused
and this is not. Pairs with a run whose plateau arrives at an epoch nobody can predict.

factor.description: Multiply the learning rate by this when the watched number stops moving.
factor.title: Factor

min_lr.description: The floor the rate will not go below. Unlike `cosine_annealing`, this one acts on evidence rather than on a schedule, so it may never fire at all - which is why it is not refused alongside `swa` and a cosine is.
min_lr.title: Min Lr

monitor.description: What to watch: `val_loss`, `train_loss`, or `val_` followed by a metric the model asks for, such as `val_dice`. Whether the number should rise or fall is worked out from its name - anything ending in `loss` is minimised. Watching something no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built, and so is watching `val_*` in a run with `validation: false`, rather than waiting for a number that never arrives.
monitor.title: Monitor

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

patience.description: Epochs to wait, with no improvement, before acting.
patience.title: Patience

ReduceLrOnPlateau.title: ReduceLrOnPlateau

Region.description:
One scored class, named as a union of the values a label map already holds.

The case this exists for is the one where overlapping classes are a *convention applied
to exclusive data* rather than a different file format. BraTS gives every voxel one of
`{0, 1, 2, 4}` and scores three regions that are unions of those values:

    enhancing tumour  of: [4]
    tumour core       of: [1, 4]
    whole tumour      of: [1, 2, 4]

The same shape appears wherever a lesion sits inside an organ - liver and tumour, kidney
and cyst, lung and nodule - and nothing new has to be read off disk for it.

`of` is a membership test, which is why nothing here has to declare the full vocabulary
of values the mask holds: a value no region mentions is simply absent from every channel.
That is also the mistake this invites, so `inspect_masks()` counts what each region
matched - a region naming a value the data does not hold is a channel of zeros, and a
channel of zeros trains to predict nothing and scores a Dice of 0 without complaining.

name.description: What this region is called. It names a channel of the output, so it is what a per-class score is reported under and what `save_class_masks` puts in a filename. Distinct from every other region's name.
name.title: Name

of.description: The label-map values belonging to this region, in any order. A voxel is in the region when its value is one of these, so regions may overlap - that is the point - and a single value is normal: BraTS's enhancing tumour is `of: [4]`. Disjoint regions are allowed and mean something useful, grouping several labels into one class and dropping the background channel; they are not a mistake and are not refused.
of.title: Of

Region.title: Region

Rim.description:
Background, object interior, object rim - three classes, one extra channel.

The cheapest signal there is: the head is one channel wider than the data's class
count and the ordinary softmax losses apply to all of it unchanged, so nothing about
the objective or the activation is special. What it costs is that the rim is taken out
of the objects, which is the trade `Separation.RIM` has the numbers for.

```yaml
separation:
  name: rim
  width: 2          # in pixels of the model's input, and not the published sweep's 3
decode:
  - name: nearest_seed
  - name: connected_components
```

name.description:
Which separation signal, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `rim` takes `width`, `flows` takes `mode`, `loss` and `weight`. A setting that belongs to the other mechanism is not refused here, it is **unwritable** - `width` under `name: flows` is an unknown key, which is the answer every typo in a specification gets.

That is this block's reason to be a block, and it was built flat first: `separation: rim` beside `rim_width`, `flow_mode`, `flow_loss` and `flow_weight`. The flat form parses, so it needs a validator and a table of which field belongs to which mechanism to refuse half of what it accepts, and it shows every reader four fields of which two can apply to them. This form shows a reader of `name: rim` one field, and the refusal is gone rather than written - `extra="forbid"` was already doing that job for every other key in the file.
name.title: Name

width.description:
How many pixels wide the rim class is, **in pixels of the model's own input** - so it means the same thing whether the image was resized or tiled, because the target is built after the resize and the augmentation rather than before (`pyplatypus#210`).

**There is a measured sweep of this quantity and it is not a sweep of this field, which is worth knowing before quoting either.** Four runs differing in nothing else scored 0.5169, 0.5486, **0.5587** and 0.5306 of instance average precision at widths 1 to 4, against a 0.0074 spread between two runs of one configuration - but that pipeline derived the rim at the *source* resolution and resized the three-class map afterwards. A Data Science Bowl case is around 520 pixels and the model reads 256, so the peak of that sweep is roughly 1.5 pixels of model input, not 3. The default is the nearest width above it. A sweep in these units has not been run.

What that sweep does establish is the shape of the trade, which is the part that transfers: **a rim wide enough to learn is wide enough to hollow the object out**, so rim Dice climbed 0.48 to 0.76 across those widths while interior Dice fell 0.90 to 0.81, and past the peak the model found *more* regions and matched fewer of them. Both halves are reported per run, because a single instance number cannot say which of them moved.
width.title: Width

Rim.title: Rim

RmsProp.description:
Adam's denominator without Adam's momentum.

Divides the step by a running average of squared gradients - `alpha` is this family's
name for Adam's `beta_2` - and leaves the direction to the raw gradient unless
`momentum` is set. Worth trying where Adam's first moment seems to be carrying the run
past a minimum.

alpha.description: Decay for the running average of the squared gradient - RmsProp's name for what Adam calls `beta_2`, and it does the same work.
alpha.title: Alpha

eps.description: Added to the denominator so a parameter whose gradient has been zero for a while does not take an enormous step. It is a guard, not a knob.
eps.title: Eps

learning_rate.description: How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an `encoder_learning_rate` is not flattened by a schedule.
learning_rate.title: Learning Rate

momentum.description: Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.
momentum.title: Momentum

name.description: Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `sgd` takes `momentum`, the Adam family takes `beta_1` and `beta_2`. `learning_rate` and `weight_decay` are accepted by all of them.
name.title: Name

weight_decay.description: Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.
weight_decay.title: Weight Decay

RmsProp.title: RmsProp

channels_from.description: For datasets that keep one channel per file - BraTS ships T1, T1ce, T2 and FLAIR per patient; 38-Cloud keeps its bands apart - one pattern per channel, in channel order, each a regular expression matched against the file names. Every pattern must match exactly one of a sample's files. Stated rather than inferred because sorting gives flair, t1, t1ce, t2: reproducible, and anatomically meaningless. A model trained with FLAIR in channel one and used on data where channel one is T1 returns a plausible answer and no error.
channels_from.title: Channels From

classes_from.description:
For masks kept as one binary file per class - the fourth way of saying what a mask's classes are, and the only one that can express classes which overlap *independently*: a vessel crossing an organ, or two annotators' masks of the same structure. One pattern per class, in class order, each a regular expression matched against a sample's mask file names, and every pattern must match exactly one file - the rules `channels_from` uses, through the same matcher.

Stated rather than inferred for the reason `channels_from` gives, with worse consequences: sorting the names is reproducible and anatomically meaningless, and a model trained with 'tumour' in channel 1 and used where channel 1 is 'oedema' answers plausibly, in range, and nothing downstream can tell.

Like `regions` this makes every channel an independent binary question - a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them - and has **no background entry**. The difference between the two is the file on disk and nothing else: `regions` derives overlap from one label map's values, which is what BraTS and the liver-and-tumour family need, and this reads overlap that was drawn separately in the first place. Exactly one of `colormap`, `labels`, `regions` and `classes_from` is given.
classes_from.title: Classes From

colormap.description: One colour per class; index in this list is the class index.
colormap.title: Colormap

column_sep.description: For `config_file`, what separates several paths inside one cell - a sample with one mask file per object, as Data Science Bowl has, or one file per channel.
column_sep.title: Column Sep

labels.description: For masks stored as label maps rather than pictures: the voxel value of each class, in class order. This is how volumes label anything - NIfTI holds integers, not colours - and how a single-channel PNG mask can be read too. Exactly one of `colormap` and `labels` is given. **Include 0 unless the masks really do fill every voxel**: a value matching no entry falls back to the first class, so a list without 0 trains the background as whatever that first class is, and `fit` refuses the combination rather than let it look plausible.
labels.title: Labels

mode.description: How the files are arranged: `nested_dirs` for one directory per sample, `config_file` for a CSV whose columns name the files. The CSV form is what to use when the data cannot be moved or copied into a layout.

regions.description: Overlapping classes, named as unions of a label map's values - the third way of saying what a mask's classes are, and the only one that lets a voxel belong to more than one. Each entry gives a `name` and the values it is made `of`. With `regions` the model's channels are independent binary questions: a sigmoid per channel rather than one softmax across them, and **no background entry**, for the same reason detection's `classes` has none. Exactly one of `colormap`, `labels` and `regions` is given. Two regions are the minimum - one region is ordinary binary segmentation, which `labels: [0, 1]` already says.
regions.title: Regions

shuffle.description: Shuffle the training data between epochs. Only the training data: validation is read in order so that two epochs measure the same thing in the same way.
shuffle.title: Shuffle

split.description: Divide `train_path` instead of naming a second folder. Nothing is written: the samples that were already discovered are partitioned, so a specification stays a description and leaves no files behind. `split_dataset()` is the tool when the CSVs are the point - to keep, to hand to a colleague, or to cite.

subdirs.description: For `nested_dirs`, the two subdirectories of each sample directory: the images and their masks. A sample may hold several mask files - one per object, as Data Science Bowl does - and they are united into one mask when read.
subdirs.title: Subdirs

target_spacing.description: Resample every volume to this many millimetres per voxel before training, then centre-crop or pad to the model's input_shape. Without it a volume is simply resized to input_shape, which gives two scans of the same anatomy different physical scale when they were acquired at different slice thicknesses - and the network has no way to know. Volumes only; ignored for 2D.
target_spacing.title: Target Spacing

test_path.description: A third set, scored only when asked. Whether it can be scored at all depends on whether it carries labels: a folder of images alone is accepted and `predict` works on it, while `evaluate` refuses it by name rather than failing two layers down on the first missing mask.
test_path.title: Test Path

train_path.description: Where the training data is. For `nested_dirs`, a directory of sample directories; for `config_file`, a CSV naming the files. With a `split`, this is the only path given and the divisions are cut from it.
train_path.title: Train Path

validation.description:
Whether this run validates at all. `false` is the third and last way of answering the question `validation_path` and `split` answer, and it has to be written down.

A final fit on every case you have, once the hyperparameters are settled, is a legitimate thing to want - and until now it meant inventing a split and ignoring the number it produced. What is *not* legitimate is arriving here by omission: a specification with neither a path nor a split is still an error, because 'I have no validation set' and 'I forgot' look identical and only one of them is a decision.

With `false`, giving `validation_path` or `split` as well is refused: they say where the validation set comes from and this says there is not one.
validation.title: Validation

validation_path.description: Optional only in the sense that `split` is the other way to get one, and `validation: false` the third. Exactly one of them, because two sources for the validation set are two places to change it.
validation_path.title: Validation Path

window.description: How values in real units are mapped to 0-1: a named window such as 'lung' or 'soft_tissue', an explicit (centre, width) pair, 'auto' for the window the file recorded - DICOM only, since NIfTI stores none - or 'full' for the whole range present. A fixed window is what makes two scans comparable: scaling each one by its own extremes lets a single bright voxel rescale everything else. Ignored for ordinary pictures, which are already 0-255. Accepted as `dicom_window` too, the name it had while DICOM was the only format that needed it.
window.title: Window

activation.description: The non-linearity between convolutions, the same one throughout.

architecture.description: Which U-shaped network. Measured on Data Science Bowl, one split, 60 epochs, the four span 0.9187 to 0.9217 of Dice - a spread of 0.0030, against 0.054 between images within any one of them, and 0.0012 from re-running one of them with another seed. On that problem the architecture is not where the result comes from. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` names one.

augmentation.description: albumentations transforms, applied to the training data only - never to validation, where the point is to measure the same thing every epoch. Each step is probed at the model's own input size while the pipeline is built, because support for volumes is uneven and a transform that cannot take one raises from inside the library.
augmentation.title: Augmentation

batch_normalization.description: Normalise between convolutions. On by default, and worth knowing about when weights are averaged: `swa` has to recompute these statistics over the training data, because an averaged weight tensor inherits them from whichever epoch was last rather than averaging them.
batch_normalization.title: Batch Normalization

batch_size.description: How many samples go through the network at once. Limited by memory rather than by the problem, and it is the first thing to lower when a 3D run will not fit. It interacts with `batch_normalization`: statistics taken over very few samples are noisy.
batch_size.title: Batch Size

block_width.description: Convolutions per block, at every level. 2 is what every U-Net paper uses and what the published weights were trained with; raising it adds depth without adding levels, which is the lever to reach for when the objects are small enough that halving the resolution again would lose them.
block_width.title: Block Width

blocks.description: How many times the resolution is halved, so how much context the deepest layer sees. `input_shape` must divide by 2^blocks. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` is given and this is not; with an `encoder`, the backbone's own depth is the ceiling.
blocks.title: Blocks

callbacks.description: Things that happen between epochs: stopping early, writing checkpoints, moving the learning rate, averaging the weights. A callback watching a number no metric will produce is refused when the specification is built rather than waited on forever, and so is one watching `val_*` in a run with no validation set.
callbacks.title: Callbacks

channels.description: How many channels the network takes: 3 for colour, 1 for greyscale, and one per sequence for multi-modal data such as the four MRI sequences in BraTS. Derived rather than declared when `channels_from` names the files, because then the data decides. Not adopted from a weights file - the data pipeline needs it before a network exists, and a specification has to be checkable offline.
channels.title: Channels

deep_supervision.description: Train every decoder depth rather than only the last, each at input resolution. `u_net_plus_plus` only, since it is the architecture with intermediate outputs to supervise.
deep_supervision.title: Deep Supervision

dropout.description: Drop this fraction during training. 0 switches it off, which is the default because these models are small enough that batch normalisation usually carries the regularisation on its own.
dropout.title: Dropout

encoder.description: A timm backbone to use as the contracting path, e.g. 'resnet34'. Leave unset for the built-in encoder, which is the only one that works in 3D.
encoder.title: Encoder

encoder_learning_rate.description: A separate, usually smaller learning rate for the layers that arrived pretrained. Whatever is ours trains at the optimizer's own rate instead - the decoder and the full-resolution stage in front of the backbone for a segmentation model, the pooled head for a classifier - because those start random. Unset means one rate for the whole network.
encoder_learning_rate.title: Encoder Learning Rate

epochs.description: How many passes over the training data. The default is deliberately small: it is enough to see that a run works and not enough to mistake for a result. With `cosine_annealing` this is also the length the schedule is spread over.
epochs.title: Epochs

filters.description: Filters in the first block, doubled at every level, so this sets the model's size more than anything else does. Adopted from the weights file when `weights` is given and this is not.
filters.title: Filters

fit.description: Set false to load weights and skip training.
fit.title: Fit

freeze_encoder.description: Keep the pretrained layers fixed for this many epochs, then train them. Lets the random part of the network settle - the decoder, or a classifier's head - before its gradients reach weights worth keeping. A number at or above `epochs` freezes them for the whole run.
freeze_encoder.title: Freeze Encoder

initialiser.description: How the weights start. The `he_*` family is scaled for ReLU-like activations and `glorot_*` for symmetric ones, so this and `activation` are a pair.

input_shape.description: Spatial size: (height, width) in 2D, (depth, height, width) in 3D.
input_shape.title: Input Shape

loss.description: The objective trained against. The `loss` column of a score table is comparable only between models trained on the same one - a Focal-Tversky of 0.05 is not better than a cross-entropy of 0.14, it is not the same question - which is why the table carries the loss's name beside it.
loss.title: Loss

metrics.description: What to report beside the loss, computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so these stay comparable across models. A callback watching `val_<metric>` is refused when nothing here will produce it.
metrics.title: Metrics

name.description: Unique within a spec; names the outputs.
name.title: Name

optimizer.description: How the weights are updated. `name` selects which one and decides which other keys this block accepts.
optimizer.title: Optimizer

pretrained.description: Load the encoder's ImageNet weights. Separate from `encoder` on purpose: naming a backbone builds that architecture, and this is the flag that reaches the network, which matters where there is no network.
pretrained.title: Pretrained

separable_conv.description: Depthwise-separable convolutions: far fewer parameters for the same shape, and a little slower to converge.
separable_conv.title: Separable Conv

spatial_dropout.description: Drop whole feature maps rather than individual activations. The right kind for images, because neighbouring pixels in one map are correlated and dropping them one at a time removes less than it appears to. Has no effect unless `dropout` is above 0.
spatial_dropout.title: Spatial Dropout

splits.description: Cut each image into a grid of tiles instead of shrinking it. One entry per spatial dimension, e.g. [2, 3] cuts into 2 rows by 3 columns. The source is read at splits * input_shape and divided; every tile is input_shape. Leave unset to resize the whole image instead. Training then shuffles in windows rather than over every tile, so one decode serves all of a sample's tiles: measured on 2048-pixel retinas cut sixteen ways, the loader costs 254 ms a tile shuffled wholesale against 49 ms this way, and a batch still draws from several sources.
splits.title: Splits

weights.description: Registry name (e.g. 'dsbowl-unet') or a path to a local checkpoint.
weights.title: Weights

data.description: Where the images and their masks are, and how to read them.

deterministic.description:
Ask torch for deterministic algorithms as well, which is the only thing that makes a run on a card repeatable - `seed` alone does not, and the field above says so.

**It is an opt-in because the cost is real and arrives late.** Some convolutions become much slower, and an operation that has no deterministic implementation raises *when it is reached* - so a run can stop ten minutes in rather than when the specification was checked. Every other refusal here happens before anything is read; this one cannot, because whether an operation has a deterministic algorithm is a fact about the installed torch and the device, not about the configuration.

Needs `seed`: constraining the algorithms while the draw still varies produces a run that is no more repeatable and only slower, so asking for it without a seed is refused rather than quietly accepted.
deterministic.title: Deterministic

models.description: One or more models, trained in turn against the same data. Names must be unique: a run is recorded under its model's name, so two models called the same thing would overwrite one record and report it as two. Several entries of the same architecture with different settings is the ordinary case - that is how a comparison is written.
models.title: Models

output_dir.description: Where a run record is written, and where `fit()` puts anything it is asked to save. Nothing is written unless something asks to write: naming this does not by itself create a directory.
output_dir.title: Output Dir

seed.description:
Makes a run repeatable as far as the arithmetic is deterministic, which goes further on some hardware than others - so it is worth knowing where it stops.

**Repeatable:** the split (`split_dataset` gives the same partition on any machine), a detector's fitted anchors, the order the data arrives in and its augmentation - including inside the loader's worker processes - and, on the processor, every number to twelve decimal places.

**Not repeatable:** a run on a CUDA device. Measured on a GTX 1070: two runs at one seed agreed to twelve decimals on the processor and differed in the fourth after a single epoch on the card, because cuDNN chooses algorithms this does not constrain. Nor across versions of this package - anything that changes the order data is drawn in changes what one seed draws, and `0.8.0a3` did exactly that.

So it is the field for comparing two of your own runs, and not for publishing a number somebody else can land on.
seed.title: Seed

Sgd.description:
The plain step, and the one that rewards being tuned.

Slower to get going than the adaptive optimisers and dependent on `learning_rate` and
usually on a schedule, in exchange for being the recipe most of the classification
literature's best numbers were produced with. `momentum` is what makes it usable;
`nesterov` without momentum is refused rather than quietly ignored.

learning_rate.description: How big a step to take. The one setting worth trying first when a run will not learn: too high and the loss moves without improving, too low and it improves too slowly to tell from not improving at all. Each parameter group decays from its own rate, so an `encoder_learning_rate` is not flattened by a schedule.
learning_rate.title: Learning Rate

momentum.description: Carry a fraction of the previous step into this one. 0 is plain gradient descent; 0.9 is the usual choice and is what makes SGD competitive with the adaptive methods.
momentum.title: Momentum

name.description: Which optimiser, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `sgd` takes `momentum`, the Adam family takes `beta_1` and `beta_2`. `learning_rate` and `weight_decay` are accepted by all of them.
name.title: Name

nesterov.description: Look ahead to where momentum is about to carry the weights before measuring the gradient. Needs `momentum` above 0, and giving it without momentum is refused rather than ignored.
nesterov.title: Nesterov

weight_decay.description: Pull weights towards zero at every step, which is L2 regularisation. Off by default because it interacts with the loss and is not free: on a small dataset it can cost more than the overfitting it prevents.
weight_decay.title: Weight Decay

Sgd.title: Sgd

SmoothL1Loss.description:
`mse` close to the truth and `l1` far from it, switching at `beta`.

The usual compromise, and the one the detector already uses on box size. At a very small
`beta` this is `l1` and at a very large one it is `mse` scaled by `beta`, which is worth
knowing before tuning it as if it were a third thing.

beta.description: Where the quadratic part ends and the linear one begins, in the target's own units. For a flow field scaled to roughly [-1, 1] the default makes the whole range quadratic, so lower it to get any of the robustness this loss is for.
beta.title: Beta

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

where.description:
Where the target means anything, and so where the error is averaged.

A continuous instance target is defined on the objects and undefined off them - there is no direction towards the centre for a pixel in no object - so the builder writes zero on the background. Measured on the 536 Data Science Bowl cases: the foreground is **13.97% of the pixels at 256x256** (13.48% at native size, 0.03% to 59.2% per case, 167 cases under 5%), so `everywhere` spends 86% of the objective on a value a single output bias satisfies exactly.

`foreground` divides by the mask's own total, which makes the number mean *average error per object voxel*. `everywhere` is the other defensible answer and is what CellPose and HoVer-Net's plain regression terms do - their background zero is a real value rather than a missing one. Both are offered and neither is guessed; `foreground` is the default because it is the reading whose number means something.

`foreground` asks the loader for the mask, which is the same mechanism `boundary` uses for its distance map. It is never read off the target: a flow field is exactly zero at every object's centre, so a mask taken from the non-zero voxels would drop precisely the seeds - and the seeds are what limits this approach (`pyplatypus#211`).
where.title: Where

SmoothL1Loss.title: SmoothL1Loss

SplitSpec.description:
How to divide one folder, when there is only one folder.

The alternative to naming `validation_path`: a researcher with a single directory
should not have to run a splitting tool and then point three paths at its output,
and nothing about that round trip was ever checked.

Nothing is written. `split_samples` partitions the samples that were already
discovered, so a specification stays a description and gains no side effect on disk.
`split_dataset()` is still the tool when you want the CSVs to keep, to hand to a
colleague or to cite.

fractions.description: Two or three: train, validation, and optionally test. The length rule is enforced by the splitting module rather than restated here - one rule, one place. A third fraction is scoreable, because it comes from annotated data.
fractions.title: Fractions

group_by.description:
**Required, and may be null.** A regular expression read against the sample key; everything sharing a group lands in exactly one split. Usually a patient, sometimes a study, a scanner or a site - whatever must not straddle the division.

Required rather than optional because the mistake it prevents is invisible. Slices of one patient in training and validation at once make validation measure memory instead of generalisation, and Dice comes out several points too high with nothing in the output to say so. An omitted field would be that choice made silently; `null` is the same choice made on purpose, which is all this asks for.
group_by.title: Group By

seed.description: The split is deterministic given the samples, the fractions, the pattern and this. A split that moves between runs makes two results incomparable and the reason for a difference impossible to find.
seed.title: Seed

SplitSpec.title: SplitSpec

StepDecay.description:
Multiply the learning rate by `factor` at fixed points in the run.

The schedule most published recipes are written in - *divide by ten at epochs 30 and
60* - which is why it is here beside the curves: reproducing somebody's result should
not require translating their staircase into a cosine.

The rate is computed from the optimiser's initial value and the number of drops so far
rather than by repeatedly multiplying what is there, so it does not drift and it is the
same whether an epoch is replayed or not.

every.description: Drop every this many epochs. Mutually exclusive with `milestones` - one of the two, never both. A period survives a change to `epochs`, where a list of milestones does not, so this is the one to prefer when the schedule is yours rather than somebody else's.
every.title: Every

factor.description: What the rate is multiplied by at each drop. 0.1 is the usual recipe's divide by ten. It must be below 1: a step schedule that raises the rate is a different idea with different arguments, and silently accepting it here would hide a typo.
factor.title: Factor

milestones.description: The epochs to drop at, 1-based, as a published recipe states them - `[30, 60]` is divide by ten at thirty and again at sixty. Mutually exclusive with `every`. Strictly increasing, and an epoch past the end of the run is refused rather than ignored, because a milestone that never fires is almost always a number that was meant to fire.
milestones.title: Milestones

min_lr.description: The floor the drops stop at, as in `reduce_lr_on_plateau`.
min_lr.title: Min Lr

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

StepDecay.title: StepDecay

StopAfter.description:
End the run on the clock, whatever the epochs say.

An epoch cap is the wrong instrument for a wall-clock budget: how long an epoch takes
is a property of the data and the shape, and the cases where this matters are exactly
the ones where that was not what anybody expected. A card shared between queued
measurements is the usual reason - a run that overshoots does not cost itself, it costs
whatever was waiting behind it.

**Stopping on the clock is not stopping on evidence**, so the weights at that moment
are whichever epoch happened to be last. Pair it with `early_stopping`'s
`restore_best`, or with `model_checkpoint`, if what the run produced matters.

hours.description: The budget, in hours. Checked at the end of each epoch, so the real limit is this plus one epoch - said here rather than discovered, because on a long arm that remainder is twenty minutes. The run's `stop_reason` names the clock, so a run that ran out of time does not read as a run that converged.
hours.title: Hours

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

StopAfter.title: StopAfter

SurfaceDiceMetric.description:
How much of each boundary lies within a tolerance of the other, rather than how much
of the volume coincides.

Dice asks about volume. `cldice` asks about connectedness. Neither asks **how far
wrong** a boundary is, and that is what is asked of a contour somebody has to approve:
the volume vignette ended on a model at Dice 0.88 whose volumes were 12% to 23% too
large, and this is the number that says so directly rather than being inferred from two
columns that disagree. It is also what `boundary` optimises and nothing here reported,
so that loss was being judged by the metric it exists to improve on.

Normalised surface Dice as published (Nikolov et al., 2018), and symmetric on purpose:
the truth's surface near the prediction is the boundary's recall, the prediction's
surface near the truth is its precision, and the single ratio weights the two by
surface size.

**The one metric here that reads the voxel spacing**, which is why it belongs in a
package that carries one. With `target_spacing` set every sample is on a common grid and
`tau` is in millimetres; without it each sample was resized independently and `tau` is
in voxels - the same pair of answers the signed distance map gives, and for the same
reason. A 0.5 mm and a 2.5 mm acquisition are not comparable in voxels at all.

Like `cldice` it is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run (`splits`) it is
reported per case by `evaluate_cases` rather than per batch.

include_background.description: False here where `dice` and `iou` default to True, and for a measured reason rather than the usual one. The background's boundary is the foreground's boundary **plus the edge of the picture**, and that edge agrees trivially between any two masks - so the background class reads high whatever the model did. Measured on four random pairs at `tau` 2: background 0.6110 to 0.7030 against foreground 0.5583 to 0.6266, higher every time, by 0.05 to 0.12. That is agreement on the field of view rather than on the object.
include_background.title: Include Background

name.description: Normalised surface Dice: the fraction of each boundary lying within `tau` of the other. A surface is a property of a whole mask, so on a tiled run (`splits`) it is reported **per case** by `evaluate_cases`, which reassembles a case's tiles first, and it is absent from the epoch history - a per-batch average of per-tile boundaries would be a number about nothing.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.
smooth.title: Smooth

tau.description: The tolerance, and it is **required because no default is honest**: a tolerance belongs to the structure and the dataset, and is conventionally the inter-observer variability for that structure - the distance two people drawing the same boundary differ by. Published values exist per organ and per challenge; take one from the protocol you are comparing against rather than from here. In millimetres when `target_spacing` puts the data on a common grid, and in voxels when it does not.
tau.title: Tau

SurfaceDiceMetric.title: SurfaceDiceMetric

Swa.description:
Average the weights over the last part of the run instead of taking the final ones.

Stochastic weight averaging. Past `start`, every epoch's weights are folded into a
running average and at the end that average becomes the model - the claim being that a
point in the middle of a flat region generalises better than the corner the last epoch
stopped in.

**Batch-normalisation statistics are recomputed afterwards**, by a pass over the
training data. They have to be: an averaged weight tensor *inherits* the statistics of
whichever epoch was last rather than averaging them, so without the pass the model is
evaluated under the wrong normalisation and scores far worse than it should, with
nothing to say why. It is the step an SWA implementation leaves out.

**What it is worth, measured.** Three seeds, 60 epochs, lesions with ambiguous edges:

```
             Dice             volume bias        |volume error|
plain        0.9639 ±0.0100   +1.71% ±12.18%     12.60% ±4.19%
swa 0.75     0.9667 ±0.0087   +2.08% ±2.15%      12.38% ±4.31%
swa 0.5      0.9640 ±0.0085   +2.78% ±3.44%      13.75% ±4.21%
```

**Dice does not move and neither does the per-case error** - both are inside the seed
noise. What moves is *reproducibility*: the volume bias of the plain runs was +4.5%,
+12.2% and -11.6% across seeds, and with averaging it was -0.1%, +4.2% and +2.1%. A
spread 5.7 times tighter, and paired per seed the distance from unbiased improved on
all three, by 7.34% at 4.9 standard errors.

Which is what averaging is supposed to do and not what one looks for in a table of
scores: a point in the middle of a flat region is the same point whichever corner the
last epoch wandered into. Read it as "the same model twice" rather than "a better
model".

No `monitor`: like `cosine_annealing` this is a function of how far through the run you
are, not of how the run is going.

learning_rate.description:
Hold the rate at this value once averaging begins. Unset leaves whatever the run was doing.

Worth setting, and the reason is the whole mechanism: averaging is only worth something while the weights are still moving. A rate that has decayed towards zero produces a set of nearly identical snapshots, and their average is the last one.
learning_rate.title: Learning Rate

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

start.description: The fraction of the run after which averaging begins - 0.75 folds the last quarter. A fraction rather than an epoch so that it survives a change to `epochs`, and the final epoch is always folded, so 1.0 averages one set of weights rather than none.
start.title: Start

start_epoch.description: Do not act before this epoch, 1-based. Mutually exclusive with `start`. This is the one to use when the warm-up is a property of the optimisation rather than of the run's length - a schedule's warm-up is fifteen epochs whether the run is 60 or 600. For `swa` that is the epoch averaging begins at, and it is the same concept `early_stopping` names with these two words.

TerminateOnCollapse.description:
End the run when the model stops predicting any foreground at all.

`terminate_on_nan`'s quiet sibling. A model that collapses to background is not
obviously broken from the numbers: with `include_background` the Dice is a mean over
class channels and the background channel is nearly perfect, so a collapsed model can
report around 0.5 while the loss falls. The run completes, the table looks plausible
and the masks are empty.

What it watches is `val_foreground`, which every epoch reports: the share of the
prediction that is not background.

floor.description: Below this share of foreground the prediction counts as collapsed. A floor rather than exactly zero, because a model predicting 0.01% foreground on a target that is 14% foreground has collapsed in every sense that matters. The default is deliberately far below any real target: this is a guard against a failure, not a quality threshold, and a floor near a real foreground share would end runs that were merely bad.
floor.title: Floor

monitor.description: Which foreground share to watch. `train_foreground` is the other one, and it answers a different question: a model collapsing on the training data has a different problem from one collapsing only on data it has not seen.
monitor.title: Monitor

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

patience.description: Epochs in a row below the floor before the run ends. An early epoch legitimately predicts almost nothing, which is why this is not 1.
patience.title: Patience

TerminateOnCollapse.title: TerminateOnCollapse

TerminateOnNaN.description:
End the run the moment the loss stops being a number.

No fields: there is nothing to decide. What it saves is the rest of a run that cannot
recover, and NaN here has causes worth knowing rather than fearing - a learning rate
far too high, a metric with `smooth: 0` meeting a class that is absent from an image,
or a skeleton-based score on an empty mask.

name.description: Which callback, and it decides which other keys this block accepts. Giving a key the chosen callback does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

TverskyLoss.description:
Dice with a thumb on the scale: miss less, or over-segment less.

`alpha` weights false negatives and `1 - alpha` false positives, so raise it when a
missed lesion costs more than a flagged healthy voxel. **At 0.5 this is Dice, but at
twice the smoothing** - measured: `tversky(alpha=0.5, smooth=1)` equals
`dice(smooth=2)` exactly. Leaving `alpha` at its default is therefore not Tversky; it
is Dice with a different floor, and that is the thing to notice when comparing runs.

alpha.description: Weight on false negatives; raising it buys recall at the cost of precision, which is the trade a screening task usually wants. The weight on false positives is 1 - alpha and is not a separate key, so the two cannot disagree. At alpha 0.5 this is Dice exactly, but only when `smooth` is 0.
alpha.title: Alpha

name.description: Which loss, and it decides which other keys this block accepts: `tversky` takes `alpha`, `focal` takes `gamma`, and giving a key the chosen loss does not have is refused by name rather than ignored.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Added to both numerator and denominator so a class absent from an image gives a finite number instead of 0/0. Leave it alone unless you know why you are moving it: raising it makes an empty class look better than it is.
smooth.title: Smooth

TverskyLoss.title: TverskyLoss

TverskyMetric.description:
A score that can be asked to care more about what was missed.

The metric form of the loss, and useful for reporting a recall-leaning number beside
the symmetric one. Moving `alpha` is the only reason to choose it: at the default it is
Dice, with the same doubling of the smoothing the loss has.

alpha.description: Weight on false negatives, with 1 - alpha on false positives - the same meaning as in the Tversky loss. At 0.5 this is Dice, so it is worth moving or not reporting at all: a Tversky metric at 0.5 beside a Dice metric is one number twice.
alpha.title: Alpha

include_background.description: Average over every class, background included. In medical images the background is often 95% of the pixels, so leaving it in flatters the score; papers usually report foreground only. Set false for that.
include_background.title: Include Background

name.description: Which metric. These are computed on the mask rather than on the objective, so they stay comparable between models trained on different losses.
name.title: Name

smooth.description: Zero is allowed here, unlike in the losses. Smoothing inflates a reported score: a class absent from an image scores a perfect 1.0 with smooth>0. Use 0 for an honest number, at the cost of NaN on absent classes.
smooth.title: Smooth

Watershed.description:
Flood the foreground from the predicted interiors, over the rim evidence as terrain.

The interiors are the markers and the model's own rim probability is the surface, so a
join lands on a ridge rather than on the midline between two seeds - which is the
information `nearest_seed` throws away when it thresholds the rim and never looks at it
again. The engine passes that probability; there is nothing to configure, because the
one defensible choice of surface is the model's own.

**Measured, and it does not pay here.** On one trained model it reaches 0.5458 against
`nearest_seed`'s 0.5561 - 0.0103 below, which is 7.8 times the 0.0013 standard deviation
of three runs of the identical configuration. Surface quality matters a great deal to
it, and to nothing: a *perfect* rim as the surface is worth +0.0132, ten times that
standard deviation, and only draws level with the decoding that ignores the surface
altogether. So the seeds decide which objects exist and the seam between them is
second-order. `pyplatypus#211`, closed measured-and-no.

minimum_area.description:
Drop an object smaller than this many pixels. 0 keeps everything, which is the default because the right floor is a property of the data rather than of the method - a nucleus at 256x256 in the Data Science Bowl runs from 4 pixels up, so a floor chosen here would silently delete the smallest real objects in one dataset while letting speckle through in another.

It is applied after the objects are formed, so it removes answers rather than changing how they were reached.
minimum_area.title: Minimum Area

name.description: Which decoding, and it decides which other keys this block accepts - `follow_flows` takes `steps` and `step_size`, the others do not. A decoding the chosen `separation` cannot feed is refused by name with both halves stated, rather than returning a label map of something else.
name.title: Name
